P1.evidence: The weakest open in the batch. Setter referenced but not read back — 'know you spoke with Kim. He kind of gave me a little bit of an overview. He said you were a very cool guy.' Standing three-part frame delivered as usual, missing what's in the way and what you need. No agreement was sought, and the prospect took the frame off him immediately: 'Feel free to ask me any question you want. The purpose is, as I told Kim, to give you the information and make sure if we have an alliance.' The open question was then never asked at all — the prospect launched into a five-minute self-briefing and the rep's next contribution was 'I appreciate you for sharing all of that.' This is the only call in the batch where P1d did not run, and it set the pattern for the rest: the prospect interviewed the product for thirty-six minutes.

P2.evidence: Nutrition was asked properly and early — 'what does your nutrition look like?' — and produced a full picture including the sweets problem and the abs-as-barometer heuristic. Age was asked, which is rare in this folder, though only in the flow of banter, and height and weight were never taken. Work was asked, but at 00:26:27, after the price had been quoted and the deal effectively lost, which is when the rep discovered he was talking to an ex-Google, ex-lawyer agency founder. The rep explicitly declined to run the training half of the baseline — 'I feel like I understand the training side of it' — on the strength of a monologue. Most consequentially, the prospect said in plain present tense 'I'm keeping having injuries' and no injury question ever followed; the rep deferred it to a future onboarding call with 'tell us where you get injured. If you've got any diagnoses, tell us that.' No sleep, no energy, no health conditions.

P3.evidence: The six-month question was asked and asked well, with the prospect's stated contentment properly acknowledged first: 'What is it that you're looking to achieve then, because you're happy with the weight... if we were to fast forward six months, what is it that you'd be happy with?' Mobility was picked up and reflected back. Then nothing. No bridge to what is actually driving it, no what-does-this-do-for-you, no who-else-does-it-impact, no legacy, no reflect-back. The waste here is unusually visible because the prospect supplied the material himself, twice and unprompted — 'there is a gap between my mental age and my biological age' and 'the worst feeling ever... is missing out. Because you will get to a point at a certain time that you can't take time back.' Both went unused.

P4.evidence: No past-attempts questions at all, on a prospect with twenty-one years of history and an unusually informative one: he hired a coach once, worked from a spreadsheet for three or four months, learned what he needed and left. That single fact is the entire commercial problem with this deal and it was never examined. He did name his own gap — 'as any new method, I strongly believe that there is a learning curve. And once you have the basic, that's it' — which is a partial P4e and also, read correctly, a statement that he intends to buy three months of instruction and then leave again.

P5.evidence: Nothing. The seventh consecutive call in this folder with no consequence frame, and the first where not even the readiness variant ran. The prospect delivered P5a for him, unprompted and vividly: 'I'm seeing people who didn't work out in the 50s, 60s, they look like a wreck. And I don't want to be there.' The rep's reply was 'How old are you?' A single follow-up — is that something you're willing to settle for, and why not — would have put a cost on the other side of a $6,000 number that was instead presented with an apology.

P6.evidence: No commitment check of any kind. Price was quoted at 00:24:31 with no belief question, no all-in question and no yes obtained. Worse than absent: the rep actively pre-framed rejection before naming the figure — 'Yeah, it probably won't be in line with your budget. I'll be honest, I'll be honest with you' — and repeated it afterwards. Phase 6 exists to establish that the prospect wants the outcome before the number lands. Here the only thing established before the number was that the rep did not expect him to buy.

P11.evidence: No close was attempted on the core offer. The rep did not ask for the business at any point; he moved from the price objection to sending a link for a $200/month product. Payment, onboarding, agreement and welcome steps were never in scope.

objection_plays.detail: The best move on the call and the only phase-adjacent work that landed. Trigger: 'I will think about the price and I will either get back to you or to Kim.' The rep challenged it head on, using the prospect's own profession as the lever: 'I know you've got a sales and marketing agency, you know how it is, right? To think about it either typically means, I'll be honest with you, I don't really want to do it, but I'll be really polite. Okay. Or it means I'm really, really not sure. But either one, it's uncertain.' It worked — the prospect praised the directness and gave a complete, honest account of exactly where he stood. That is precisely what the play is for. The rep then abandoned it. None of the remaining moves ran: no can-this-get-you-there, no what's-actually-preventing-you, no thinking-isn't-the-problem-deciding-is, no man-you-want-to-be. Having earned total candour, he used it to identify a cheaper product rather than to close.

Trigger flagged by the prospect from his opening minute — 'budget-wise, because I need to circle this internally after' — and again before the quote, and again after it. Not one move of the play ran. No isolation, no should-I-versus-how frame, no permission question, none of the six financial-picture questions, and no payment plan offered despite this rep having structured 50/50 splits twice earlier in the week. Beyond omission, the rep ran the play in reverse: he devalued the offer pre-emptively with 'it probably won't be in line with your budget' before quoting, agreed with the objection when it came — 'As I said, it is substantial' — and then reinforced it with 'it's probably not in your budget.' A prospect who had explicitly asked to be given the number so he could evaluate it was told twice not to expect to afford it.

The cheaper-alternative gap, in the form the script most needs an answer for, and this time the rep conceded the ground and supplied the alternative himself. The prospect stated the choice plainly — 'either to choose a different service that is costing me less or... To try to build something again on my own, like plan-wise' — and the response was 'I can shoot you over the middle ground.' Compare the Mike Bennett call the same day, where the same objection produced an honest disqualification, and the Galal Beshir call, where a prospect's prior self-directed success was reframed into evidence the coaching would work. This rep has demonstrated a better answer to this objection twice in one week and did not use it here. The structural point stands: with no scripted play, the response depends entirely on which instinct the rep reaches for on the day.

Rejection of the offer's core positioning, with no scripted play and no response. The prospect drew a distinction the whole product rests on and placed himself on the wrong side of it: 'I love the fact that you... you're not coaching, you're mentoring, and I think it's very much relevant to people who are less familiar with the exercise kind of a world... they do need a mentor, I less need a mentor, I need more of a coach.' He also asked to buy components rather than the system. The rep agreed with the terminology point and moved on. Nothing was said about why an experienced trainee still needs accountability, which is the one argument available and the one the Galal Beshir call proved this rep can make.

notes: A high-value prospect was allowed to run the entire call and was then talked out of the offer by the person selling it. The open question never got asked, the deep phases never ran, and the price was bracketed by two unprompted statements that it would not fit his budget. The single bright spot — the challenge to 'think about it' — shows the capability is there and was deployed once, thirty seconds too late to be used for anything. Two specific coaching instructions. First, never pre-declare affordability; ask instead. Second, when a self-sufficient prospect says he needs a coach rather than a mentor, that is an invitation to sell the accountability pillar, not a cue to open the $200 product. The wider issue is not coachable at rep level: with no scripted play for a functioning cheap alternative, and a $200 tier available to reach for, the path of least resistance from a $6,000 objection is a 97% discount.
